topic: The Invention of the Printing Press
setting: A short talk in a world history class about Gutenberg and the early printing press.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk in a world history class.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Before the mid-1400s in Europe, books were copied by hand, mostly by monks and professional scribes.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: That made books rare and expensive, so few people outside the elite could own one.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz combined movable metal type, oil-based ink, and a press adapted from wine presses.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: His workshop produced the famous forty-two-line Bible, one of the first major books printed in the West.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: The key idea was reusable type: once letters were cast, they could be rearranged for new pages instead of carving each page from scratch.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Within decades, printing shops spread across Europe, and the cost of books fell sharply.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Cheaper books helped literacy grow and sped the spread of scientific ideas, religious debates, and news.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Of course, printing did not invent writing—China and Korea had earlier printing traditions—but Gutenberg’s system transformed European publishing.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: So when we talk about an information revolution in early modern Europe, this technology is usually at the center of the story.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next lecture we’ll look at how printed pamphlets shaped politics in the sixteenth century.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.

questions.narrator_text: What is the talk mainly about?

options.text: How monks built wine presses for monasteries
Gutenberg’s printing press and how it changed book production in Europe
How to cast metal for jewelry
Why the Bible was never printed

questions.explanation: The professor explains Gutenberg’s movable type system and its impact on European books and literacy.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—wine presses are only mentioned as a model for the press mechanism.
questions.correctAnswer: Gutenberg’s printing press and how it changed book production in Europe

questions.narrator_text: According to the professor, what made books rare before the mid-1400s in Europe?

options.text: Only farmers were allowed to read
They were copied by hand and were expensive
Paper had not been invented yet

questions.explanation: She says books were copied by hand, making them rare and expensive.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing B—paper is not the reason she gives.
questions.correctAnswer: They were copied by hand and were expensive

questions.narrator_text: What does the professor say was the key idea of Gutenberg’s system?

options.text: Hiring more scribes instead of using machines
Carving a new wooden page for every book forever
Reusable movable type that could be rearranged for new pages

questions.explanation: She emphasizes reusable type that could be rearranged instead of carving each page from scratch.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing B—that describes the older, slower approach.
questions.correctAnswer: Reusable movable type that could be rearranged for new pages

questions.narrator_text: What can be inferred about earlier printing outside Europe?

options.text: China and Korea had earlier printing traditions, but Gutenberg’s system transformed European publishing
No culture had ever printed anything before Gutenberg

questions.explanation: She notes earlier traditions in China and Korea while stressing Gutenberg’s impact in Europe.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—she explicitly rejects that idea.
questions.correctAnswer: China and Korea had earlier printing traditions, but Gutenberg’s system transformed European publishing
